AI Compass

AI quiz with answers: 30 questions for beginners

Choose an answer to see whether it is right and why. Two questions for each lesson.

Lesson 1: What is AI?

1. What does “Artificial Intelligence” (AI) mean?

Show the answer

Right answer: Computer systems that do tasks which usually need human intelligence

AI means computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human intelligence: understanding speech, recognising faces, translating text. Not every automatic program is AI: a timer that switches on the lights just follows fixed steps. And today's AI has no feelings, and it can definitely make mistakes.

2. A chess program can beat any human champion, but it can't recognise a cat in a photo. What kind of AI is it?

Show the answer

Right answer: Narrow AI: it is built for one kind of task

Today's AI is narrow: each system is built for a certain kind of task, so being brilliant at chess says nothing about photos. Nothing is broken, and it's still AI. A general AI (AGI) would be able to learn any intellectual task a human can, and a chess program is nowhere near that.

Lesson 2: Machine Learning

3. How is machine learning different from ordinary programming?

Show the answer

Right answer: The computer learns patterns from examples, not just rules a person wrote

In machine learning, we give the computer lots of examples (say, thousands of photos labelled “cat” or “dog”) and it works out the patterns itself, so it can handle new photos too. In ordinary programming, a person writes every rule. Machine learning runs on phones as well, for example in face unlock.

4. A model gets almost every training example right, but fails badly on new photos it has never seen. What is this called?

Show the answer

Right answer: Overfitting: it memorised examples, not the pattern

This is overfitting, like learning test answers by heart without understanding the topic. Underfitting is the opposite problem: a model too simple to do well even on its training examples. Testing on new data is how we notice overfitting, not what causes it.

Lesson 3: Neural Networks

5. What does the “deep” in “deep learning” mean?

Show the answer

Right answer: The neural network has many layers, one after another

A deep neural network has many layers between the input and the output, and training such networks is called deep learning. “Deep” describes the shape of the network, not deep thoughts or deep understanding.

6. In a network that recognises photos, what do the first layers usually detect?

Show the answer

Right answer: Simple things, like edges and spots of colour

The first layers find simple patterns such as edges. The middle layers combine them into shapes and parts, and the last layers recognise whole objects. Spotting a whole cat in one step would be far too hard for a single layer.

Lesson 4: Generative AI & Chatbots

7. How does a chatbot like ChatGPT write its answers?

Show the answer

Right answer: It predicts a likely next word again and again, using patterns learned from text

Chatbots run on large language models. They build an answer one small piece of text (a “token”) at a time, each time predicting what is likely to come next. That's why they sound so fluent, but sounding confident is not the same as being right.

8. Which of these is generative AI?

Show the answer

Right answer: An app that writes a poem from a one-line request

Generative AI creates new content: text, images, music, code or video. The other three are AI too, but they sort, recognise or predict. They don't create anything new.

Lesson 5: AI in Everyday Life

9. Which of these everyday things usually uses AI?

Show the answer

Right answer: Video recommendations on YouTube or TikTok

Recommendation systems learn from what you watch, like and skip, and guess what you'll want to see next. A calculator, an alarm clock and a microwave timer just follow fixed rules: they're useful, but they don't learn or adapt to you.

10. Your feed shows you more and more videos that match what you already like and believe. What is this called?

Show the answer

Right answer: A filter bubble

When a recommendation system keeps showing you more of the same, you can end up in a filter bubble and rarely see other topics or views. Searching for new topics and following different voices helps you get out. A deepfake is a fake photo, video or voice, and a hallucination is when a chatbot makes something up.

Lesson 6: AI Ethics & Safety

11. A face-recognition system was trained mostly on photos of people with light skin. What is the most likely problem?

Show the answer

Right answer: It may be less accurate for people with darker skin

This is called AI bias. AI learns from its data, and it can't fill in what's missing by itself. If some groups of people are under-represented, the system can be less accurate or unfair to them. Researchers have found exactly this problem in real face-recognition systems, which is why diverse, balanced data matters.

12. Which of these is the safest thing to type into an online AI chatbot?

Show the answer

Right answer: A general question, like “How do volcanoes work?”

What you type into a chatbot may be stored and sometimes used to improve the AI. Never share passwords or personal details like your full name, address or school, and don't share other people's private messages either.

Lesson 7: How Computers See

13. To a computer, what is a black-and-white photo?

Show the answer

Right answer: A grid of numbers, one for each pixel

A computer stores a picture as pixels, and each pixel is just a number: in a greyscale picture, 0 is black, 255 is white, and the numbers in between are greys. A colour pixel has three numbers, for red, green and blue. Finding objects in all those numbers is exactly what vision models have to learn.

14. A small grid of numbers slides over a picture, and at each spot the numbers under it are multiplied and added up. What is this called?

Show the answer

Right answer: A convolution

This sliding and adding is a convolution, and the small grid is a filter. Where the picture has the pattern the filter looks for, such as an edge, the sum is big. A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns the numbers of its own filters from examples.

Lesson 8: Learning by Trial and Error

15. In reinforcement learning, how does an agent find out which actions are good?

Show the answer

Right answer: From the rewards it gets after trying different actions

Nobody shows a reinforcement learning agent the right moves. It acts, gets a reward (a number that says how well it did, like points in a game) and slowly works out which actions bring the most reward over time. Learning from labelled examples is supervised learning.

16. Your music app mostly plays songs you already love, but now and then it slips in something completely new. What is it doing with the new song?

Show the answer

Right answer: Exploration: trying something new to learn more

Trying something new to learn more is exploration; playing what already works is exploitation. An agent (or an app) that only exploits can get stuck with “good enough”, so a good one explores a small part of the time. Nothing is being hacked: the app is learning what else you might like.

Lesson 9: How Chatbots Write

17. Before a chatbot can work with your message, what does it cut the text into?

Show the answer

Right answer: Tokens: words and parts of words

Text is cut into tokens, such as short words, parts of longer words and punctuation marks, and each token gets a number. “Unbelievable” might become “un”, “believ” and “able”. So to the model, your message is a list of numbers.

18. What happens when you turn up a chatbot's temperature setting?

Show the answer

Right answer: Its word choices get more random and creative

Temperature changes how the model picks the next token. At a low temperature it almost always takes the most likely one (safe, but a bit dull); at a high temperature, unlikely tokens get more chances (more creative, but more mistakes). It has nothing to do with speed, mood or fact-checking.

Lesson 10: Creative AI

19. How does a diffusion model, a common kind of image generator, make a picture?

Show the answer

Right answer: It starts from random noise and removes it step by step

A diffusion model learns to remove noise. To make a picture, it starts from pure noise and cleans it up in many small steps, guided by your prompt, until a new image appears. It doesn't glue pieces of photos together or look the picture up: it builds a new one from the patterns it learned.

20. A GAN, an earlier kind of image generator from 2014, trains two networks against each other. What do they do?

Show the answer

Right answer: One makes fake images, the other tries to spot the fakes

In a generative adversarial network (GAN), a generator makes fakes, like a forger, and a discriminator tries to tell them from real images, like a detective. Each one improves by competing with the other, until the fakes are hard to spot. GANs were introduced in 2014 by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues.

Lesson 11: Can You Trust AI?

21. In 2018, news reports revealed that Amazon had dropped an experimental hiring tool. What was wrong with it?

Show the answer

Right answer: It was biased against women: it learned from past CVs

The tool learned from ten years of CVs that mostly came from men, and it learned that unfairness: it marked down CVs that mentioned women's activities, such as a women's chess club. An AI copies the patterns of its history, unfair ones included, which is why hiring tools need careful testing and people checking them.

22. A face-unlock system is right 95% of the time in tests. Why might that not be good enough?

Show the answer

Right answer: It may fail much more often for some groups of people

One overall number can hide big differences. If most test photos showed one group of people, the system could be right almost every time for them and wrong far more often for others. Good testing checks different groups and unusual cases, not just the average.

Lesson 12: Your AI Toolkit

23. “You are a geography teacher. Explain how volcanoes erupt to my class of 14-year-olds.” Which of these ingredients of a good prompt is missing?

Show the answer

Right answer: The format: how the answer should look

The prompt has a role (a geography teacher), a task (explain how volcanoes erupt) and context (a class of 14-year-olds). It doesn't say how the answer should look: five bullet points, a short story, a quiz? Adding the format, and maybe an example, makes the answer far more useful.

24. A chatbot gives you a great quote for your essay, with a link to its source. What should you do before you use it?

Show the answer

Right answer: Open the source and check that the quote is really there

Chatbots sometimes make up quotes, and even sources. Open the link and check that the source exists and really says that. Asking the chatbot “are you sure?” isn't a check: it may just sound sure again.

Lesson 13: Data: The Fuel of AI

25. Why do data scientists put some examples aside as a “test set” before training?

Show the answer

Right answer: To check the model fairly on examples it has never learned from

A model can memorise its training examples, so testing on them says little. A test set it never saw shows how it will do on new, real examples. Speed isn't the point, and the test set should be ordinary examples, not only the hard ones.

26. A class survey says one student is 150 years old. What should happen before a model is trained on it?

Show the answer

Right answer: The value should be checked and fixed or removed: it's almost certainly a mistake

A model can't tell a mistake from a fact: it learns from both. Cleaning the data (fixing or removing impossible values) comes first. One bad value doesn't spoil the whole survey.

Lesson 14: How Apps Choose for You

27. A music app suggests a song because people with listening history like yours loved it. What is this idea called?

Show the answer

Right answer: Collaborative filtering

Collaborative filtering recommends what similar people liked, without needing to know what the song is about. A Turing test is about telling people from machines, gradient descent is how many models train, and data cleaning fixes messy data.

28. Which of these usually tells a video app the most about what you like?

Show the answer

Right answer: How long you actually watch before scrolling away

Apps learn most from what you do: watching a video through says “more of this” louder than almost anything else, and a quick skip is a strong “no”. Your phone's colour or your account name say very little about your taste.

Lesson 15: Plan Your Own AI Project

29. Your school's bins need sorting: paper always goes in the blue bin. What's the best first step?

Show the answer

Right answer: Ask whether a simple rule already solves it, before reaching for AI

Good projects start with the problem. If a clear rule works, it's easier to build, check and explain than a model. AI is worth it when the rule is hard to write down but easy to show with examples. Collecting personal data the project doesn't need is never a good start.

30. You want an app that spots sick leaves. Which training data is best?

Show the answer

Right answer: Hundreds of photos of many plants, both healthy and sick, in different light

A model needs varied examples of every answer it must give. With only healthy leaves it can never learn what “sick” looks like, and twenty photos of one plant teach it that plant, not leaves in general.
